Search record lists it as Creativity & Cognition 2026 proceedings, DOI 10.1145/3803784.3816851. PDF metadata creation date 2026-05-21.
source.title_on_document: Two-Player Alternate Uses Test: A Controlled Testbed for Interactive Human–AI and Human–Human Co-Creation

supplement.where: No supplementary material or online appendix is referenced. The paper links source code (https://github.com/BabakHemmatian/AI-creativity) and a live demo (https://co-creativity.onrender.com/) on p. 2, and says platform, code, and dataset are released (abstract, p. 1).
supplement.holds: Nothing referenced. Utility ratings were collected but 'utility results are available on request' (p. 4, Section 3.4). Full-sample arm means by partner condition are not printed anywhere in the PDF.

paper_design_summary: In an in-person pilot, 62 UIUC students each completed three 4-minute two-player Alternate Uses Test chat sessions in randomized order: with another human (HUM), with a GPT-4 partner (GPT), and a non-interactive condition (CON) in which they read one of three pre-rated seed sets (GPT-4 ideas, highly creative human ideas, or uncreative human ideas), assigned between participants. After each chat participants curated the best uses in a survey tab, and 226 Prolific workers rated the 1,923 ideas for originality on a 1-5 scale. A linear mixed model compares originality across partner types.

studies.label: In-person pilot of the two-player AUT platform (HUM vs GPT vs CON, within-subject)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the three partner conditions (HUM, GPT, CON) within person; target objects (book, fork, tin can) counterbalanced across sessions; the CON seed set (gpt_con, high_con, low_con) assigned between participants (the paper does not say this sub-assignment was random and calls it uneven).
assignment.quote: Each participant completed three co-creation sessions within-subject in randomized order: human–human (HUM), human–GPT-4 (GPT), and non-interactive (CON for “constant”).
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 3.2; also p. 3, Figure 1 caption ('three randomized 4-minute co-creation sessions')
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration of the pilot is mentioned; the conclusion calls the platform 'pre-registerable' (p. 7, Section 7).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions reported. Every participant does all three partner conditions, so all 62 appear in each within-person arm by design. Figure 3 (p. 6) prints subject-level n by BAS Drive group: CON 32 + 30, GPT 32 + 29, HUM 32 + 30, which implies one participant missing from the GPT subject-level means; the paper does not explain. The outsourcing correlation in HUM uses n = 20 (p. 5). CON sub-arms: Figure 1 prints n = 21 for each of gpt_con, high_con, low_con and its text alternative says '~21 participants each', while Section 4.3 says the sub-arms were 'unevenly assigned' (p. 6); 3 x 21 = 63 does not match N = 62.
participants.who: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign students, in-person sessions for course credit; 19 male, 42 female, 1 non-binary; English-speaking (p. 7, Limitations)
participants.country: United States (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; country not named in the text)
participants.quote: Sixty-two University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign students signed up for in-person sessions in exchange for course credit (19 male, 42 female, 1 non-binary).
participants.locator: p. 3, Section 3.2; N = 62 also in abstract (p. 1) and Figure 1 caption (p. 3)

ai_tool.name_model: gpt-4 via OpenAI chat-completions API, temperature 0.7, max_tokens 3000
ai_tool.how_used: GPT-4 acts as a live chat partner generating alternate uses with the participant in a shared chat, with server-enforced strict turn-taking. Its prompt adds guardrails: one idea per turn, no preambles, single-sentence responses; a token-overlap filter rejects responses overlapping more than 50 percent with any prior message (p. 3, AI configuration). Participants are told the partner is AI. In the gpt_con CON sub-arm, participants instead read 16 pre-generated GPT-4 ideas (ideas supplied, no interaction).

task.description: Two-player Alternate Uses Test: generate unusual uses for a target object (book, fork, tin can; counterbalanced) in a shared chat, then curate the 'best' creative uses inspired by the chat in a separate survey tab (Figure 1 says 'Curate best 5'). Half of the participants also did a 2-minute solo AUT before the sessions and half after; no solo-AUT results are reported.
task.duration: 4-minute chat per session, three sessions; solo AUT 2 minutes

outcomes.name: Crowd-rated originality of ideas from the interactive sessions (GPT vs HUM)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Originality ('how unlikely others would be to generate the idea') on a 5-point Likert scale by 226 Prolific workers (Figure 1 says 225), median 6 ratings per idea, range 5-12 (p. 4, Section 3.4). Analysis: LMM with fixed effects of partner type, non-interactive assignment, and their interaction, random intercepts for subject, item-within-subject, and rater (p. 4, Section 4). Robustness: TOST equivalence test and Bayesian re-estimation with Normal(0,1) prior. 'Top-quality rate' and 'failure rate' variants are mentioned only for the BAS Drive interaction (p. 5). The scored ideas were curated in a survey tab right after the chat; the data flow box says the 1,928 ideas were 'generated in chat + curated' (Figure 1, p. 3), so it is not clear whether rated ideas include the partner's (AI's or other human's) own ideas. Utility was also rated but not reported.

contrasts.reported: β_{GPT−HUM} = −0.11, SE = 0.13, 95% CI [−0.37, +0.16], p = .42; TOST bounded maximum credible effect at |β| ≤ 0.33; Bayesian BF01 = 10.95, posterior median +0.06, 95% credible interval [−0.06, +0.20]. Subgroup subject-level means (Figure 3, Welch t-tests): low BAS Drive GPT 3.20 (n = 32) vs HUM 3.10 (n = 32), p = 0.32; high BAS Drive GPT 3.48 (n = 29) vs HUM 3.29 (n = 30), p = 0.08.

contrasts.control_arm: CON (pooled over gpt_con, high_con, low_con seed sets)
contrasts.reported: No full-sample GPT vs CON estimate printed. Interaction β_{BAS-Drive × GPT-vs-CON} = +0.20, 95% CI [+0.05, +0.38], p = .034, BF10 = 3.37; same direction on top-quality rate (p = .033) and failure rate (p = .030). Figure 3 subject-level means: low BAS Drive CON 3.44 (n = 32) vs GPT 3.20 (n = 32), p = 0.06; high BAS Drive CON 3.24 (n = 30) vs GPT 3.48 (n = 29), Δ = +0.25, p = .046, d = +0.53 (Welch t-test on subject-level means; bars mean ± 95% CI). Grand mean = 3.29.

outcomes.name: Originality in later HUM and GPT sessions by the CON seed set seen first
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Crowd-rated originality (1-5) of ideas from the HUM and GPT sessions, restricted to participants whose first session was CON; compares the seed set seen in that first session (gpt_con = GPT-4 ideas, high_con, low_con). Seed exposure is for a different target object. Exploratory; the authors note CON sub-arms were unevenly assigned. The number of participants in this subsample is not given.
outcomes.delay: Later sessions in the same visit

contrasts.control_arm: CON (high_con) seen first: 16 highly creative human ideas
contrasts.reported: Seed-set effect F(2, 1963) = 4.68, p = .009; β_{high vs gpt} = +0.32, p = .016 (higher subsequent originality after high_con than after gpt_con). No SE printed.

outcomes.name: Originality of ideas curated in the CON session by seed set (manipulation check)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Crowdsourced originality of CON-session ideas, which participants curated after reading a pre-rated seed set. The paper uses it as a manipulation check of the seed-set quality gradient, so it largely reflects the seed ideas rather than participant production.

contrasts.reported: low_con < gpt_con < high_con; β_{low−gpt} = −0.48, β_{high−gpt} = +0.23, both p < .001. No SE printed.

sample_overlap.locator: Seed ideas for high_con and low_con come from Stevenson et al. (2022) (p. 3), but these are ideas, not shared participants.

company_involvement.description: No company funding or staff involvement stated. One author lists the affiliation 'Alinea' (p. 1); its type is not stated. OpenAI's API supplies the GPT-4 partner.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author list; p. 3, AI configuration

data_and_code.data_url: https://github.com/BabakHemmatian/AI-creativity (the paper says the dataset is released; no separate data URL is printed)

eligibility.reason: Within-person design with randomized order of a GPT-4 chat partner, a human partner, and a non-interactive condition (p. 3, Section 3.2), so GPT vs HUM is a randomized ai_vs_active contrast. 62 students participated and the dataset covers all 62 (p. 2, contributions; p. 3), above the 50 threshold but not by much; Figure 3 shows 61 participants with GPT subject-level means. Outcome is crowd-rated originality of the ideas curated right after each chat (p. 4). Caveats: the paper calls the pilot exploratory; the rated ideas may include partner-generated ideas from the chat; the main estimate is from a rating-level mixed model.

one_line_finding: Among 62 students, originality of ideas from a 4-minute AUT chat with a GPT-4 partner was statistically equivalent to that with a human partner (β_{GPT−HUM} = −0.11, SE = 0.13, 95% CI [−0.37, +0.16], p = .42; BF01 = 10.95), p. 4, Section 4.1.
open_questions: Were the rated ideas only the participant's curated list, or also the partner's chat contributions (Figure 1: '1,928 ideas, generated in chat + curated')? If AI-written ideas are included, the GPT arm's score partly measures GPT-4 output.
Counts conflict: 1,928 ideas (pp. 2-3) vs 1,923 distinct rated ideas (pp. 4, 7); 226 raters (p. 4) vs 225 (Figure 1); CON sub-arms n = 21 each (Figure 1) vs N = 62 and 'unevenly assigned' (p. 6).
Was the CON seed-set sub-assignment random? The paper says only 'assigned between participants'.
S1-O2 mixes later HUM sessions (no AI) and GPT sessions (AI available); coding it as after_ai is a judgment call.
HUM sessions pair two participants, so HUM outcomes are not independent across the dyad; the paper does not say how dyads were formed.
notes: No full-sample arm means or SDs by partner condition are printed; only the GPT−HUM LMM coefficient and subgroup subject-level means in Figure 3 (read from the figure labels at high zoom). Solo AUT done before or after the sessions (a possible after-AI outcome) is collected but no results are reported. Other reported analyses are trait correlates (random-forest importance of RMET and BAS, Figure 2; RMET vs within-subject range of originality r = +0.27, p = .037; self-reported outsourcing vs originality in HUM r = −0.504, p = .024, n = 20), which are moderators rather than AI contrasts and are not listed as outcomes. No diversity outcome.
